builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models
summary: The method replaces fp16 weight storage and single-order multiple-choice evaluation with 6-bit round-to-nearest quantized weights plus averaging over up to four cyclic permutations of answer options. The cost is a multiplicative inference pass increase (up to 4x forward passes) traded against roughly 2.7x memory reduction from 6-bit weights, priced jointly as weight-bytes-read times passes. What can fail: the findings rest on two small models, a simulated quantizer, 300 items per benchmark, and an inconclusive noise control on slot skew, so the +1.8-point anomaly at 6 bits and the cost-matched decision table may not transfer to other models, real quantization kernels, or larger evaluation sets.
rationale: The recipe is cheap to implement and directly targets constrained-memory single-GPU deployment, but its evidence base is two small models with simulated quantization and small benchmark samples, so it warrants a workload-specific validation run before production adoption.

claims.statement: The method replaces fp16 weight storage and single-order multiple-choice evaluation with 6-bit round-to-nearest quantized weights plus averaging over up to four cyclic permutations of answer options. The cost is a multiplicative inference pass increase (up to 4x forward passes) traded against roughly 2.7x memory reduction from 6-bit weights, priced jointly as weight-bytes-read times passes. What can fail: the findings rest on two small models, a simulated quantizer, 300 items per benchmark, and an inconclusive noise control on slot skew, so the +1.8-point anomaly at 6 bits and the cost-matched decision table may not transfer to other models, real quantization kernels, or larger evaluation sets.
Averaging four cyclic option orders recovers +12.6 accuracy points at 4 bits for Qwen3-0.6B (+5.3 at fp16); 6-bit weights lose no accuracy versus fp16.
